first.rationale: Three concurrent pressures exist, but only one experiment slot is available this week, so the choice should target the objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue) rather than react to competitor noise. Promotional pricing (memory_73) is the most tempting reactive move given competitor entry pricing, but matching aggressive discounting risks attracting low-quality, price-sensitive accounts and could erode qualified revenue and brand positioning long-term — this needs verification against the original record before ruling out or in. Onboarding/signup simplification (memory_31, memory_86) directly addresses two of the three observed declines (activation and onboarding completion) with a previously-observed durable, low-risk lift, and doesn't require racing to the bottom on price. I verify memory_73 to check whether promotional pricing's 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' distinguished qualified vs. unqualified revenue and considered retention/margin effects, since that's the highest-risk option relative to the stated objective. I verify memory_31 since it's the older of the two onboarding memories and is central to the intended action, to confirm the effect was durable and not a novelty/measurement artifact. Given competing pressures could be compounding (e.g., competitor pricing itself may be suppressing activation/onboarding by pulling weaker-fit signups), I flag downstream risk and keep the experiment at standard scale rather than broad rollout, preserving the option to pivot toward pricing or activation messaging next cycle if this test doesn't move the needle.

final.rationale: The archive check paid off decisively: exp_73 shows the consolidated memory's framing of promotional pricing as an 'effective response' was dangerously incomplete — the +18% qualified revenue figure masked a -12% 30-day retention collapse, meaning the acquired cohort doesn't survive first renewal. The original source explicitly warns not to generalize discounting as sustainable growth. Given the primary objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, and a competitor is currently running exactly this failure mode (aggressive entry pricing), matching them would likely replicate the same short-lived, unprofitable cohort — this is ruled out. exp_31 confirms signup simplification is real and durable for SMB: signup +15%, activation +9%, retention nearly flat (-1%), qualified revenue +4% — a small but genuine, non-cannibalizing gain. This directly addresses two of the three current problems (activation down 6%, onboarding completion down 4%) without the sustainability trap seen in pricing. I'm using memory_31 (now source-verified) as the core justification and memory_86 (onboarding shortening) as corroborating but still-unverified support for the same directional lever. I keep scale at standard_experiment rather than broad_rollout because: (1) the original result is 76 days old and conditions have shifted (new competitive pressure, broader activation decline suggesting possible other causes), (2) exp_31 explicitly notes it 'holds on SMB; not replicated on other segments,' so generalizing further without a fresh read risks the same overgeneralization mistake just uncovered in exp_73. Referral incentives, activation messaging, and enterprise sales-assist remain unverified alternatives for future slots — decisive but not proof against error, given only two memories could be checked this week.
